1. Overview

Did you know that it has been predicted that by the year 2058, the number of Australians who will be 85 years and above will have risen to over 1.5 million from the amount of 515,700 in 2019? Imagine the contribution that a support worker can make to the lives of these special people and the wisdom that can be gained from their collective experiences!

2. Principles and models of support in aged care

Connect

A. PriNciple 1 (LG p11)

Involves the standards that must be achieved for a care provider to be accredited. There must be an appropriate management system, adequate staffing and organisation so that services are effective and focus on continuous improvement.

B. PriNciple 2 (LG p11)

The provision of client-focused personal and health care where the client is involved in decisions about their care.

C. PriNciple 3 (LG p11)

Clients will be assisted to retain their personal, civic and consumer rights to be able to be in control of their lives.

D. PriNciple 4 (LG p11)

The provision of an environment where the client feels safe and mental and physical wellbeing is promoted (Royal Commissions, 2014) (CBCS, 2023).

A. Principle 1
Care providers must meet certain standards to be approved. This includes having good systems in place, enough trained staff, and being organised. They must also keep trying to improve the way they deliver services.

B. Principle 2
Clients should be at the centre of their care. They should be involved in making decisions about their personal and health care.

C. Principle 3
Clients should be supported to keep their rights and stay in control of their own lives, including making their own choices.

D. Principle 4
Care should be given in a place where clients feel safe, and where their mental and physical health is supported.

4. Person-centered approach and Positive Effect

4. Person-centered approach (LG p12) Connect CHCAGE013 And Connect CHCDIS020

This approach keeps the individual person at the center of all decisions made about their care.

Each person is treated respectfully, and the aged care workers actively try to understand what is important to the person and their family.

  • Individual Focus: Prioritize the person's needs, treating them as an individual, not just their condition.
  • Decision Involvement: Involve the person in decisions about their life and care.
  • Consideration of Diversity: Take into account the person's life experience, age, gender, culture, heritage, language, beliefs, and identity.
  • Flexibility: Provide flexible services tailored to the person's wishes, priorities, and right to self-determination.

Positive Effect : This empowers people to feel like they have control over their life and can make their own choices.

5. Strengths-Based Approach

5. Strengths-Based Approach: Acknowledge the person's strengths, focusing on what they can do first, and providing help as needed.

Inclusion of Support Networks: Include the person's support networks as partners in the care process.

Central Role in Planning: Place the person at the center of planning and goal-setting, ensuring goals reflect their priorities and are developed in consultation with them.

6. Empowerment and Positive Effect

6. Empowerment: Support and enable the person to maintain control over their life, upholding their autonomy.

Positive Effect : This makes people feel better about themselves and more in control of their lives.

CHCAGE013 / *CHCDIS020*

7. Social Role Valorisation (SRV) and Positive Effect

7 -Social Role Valorisation (SRV) - This is about helping people who are disadvantaged feel valued and included in society.

Positive Effect: It helps the person recognize their worth and the contributions they can make to their community.

8. Rights-based approach

8. Rights-based approach (LG p12)

  • This means that everyone, no matter their age, has rights. Caregivers must make sure to support and respect these rights.
  • This is achieved by encouraging active decision making, where the person is given the relevant information and can then make an informed choice.
  • Respect for Preferences: Care should be based on what the person thinks is important, respecting their own values and choices.

Practical actions the 7 Strengthened Aged Care Quality Standards

Standard 1 – The Individual

I understand the people I care for and support them in choices that impact their lives.

Ask and respect individual preferences Ask residents how they prefer to be addressed, their daily routines, and cultural or personal preferences, and follow these where possible.

Support choice and independence Offer choices in daily activities such as meals, clothing, bathing times, and activities rather than making decisions for the person.

Maintain dignity and privacy Close doors or curtains during personal care, explain what you are doing, and gain consent before providing care.

Standard 2 – The Organisation

I feel empowered to do my job well.

Follow workplace policies and procedures Read and comply with organisational policies for care delivery, safety, infection control, and incident reporting.

Report risks, incidents, and concerns Promptly report hazards, near misses, incidents, or concerns about care using the organisation’s reporting system.

Participate in training and communication Attend mandatory training, handovers, and team meetings to stay informed and deliver safe, consistent care.

Standard 3 – The Care and Services

I understand who I’m caring for and what is important to them.

Use care plans to guide your work Read and follow each individual’s care plan before providing care and check for updates or changes.

Communicate clearly and respectfully Share relevant information with colleagues during handovers and listen to residents and families about changing needs.

Provide care according to assessed needs Deliver only the services outlined in the care plan and report any changes in health, behaviour, or wellbeing.

Standard 4 – The Environment

I create a safe and supportive environment.

Maintain a clean and safe environment Keep walkways clear, clean spills promptly, and ensure equipment is stored and used safely.

Follow infection prevention and control practices Perform hand hygiene correctly, use personal protective equipment (PPE) as required, and follow cleaning procedures.

Identify and report environmental hazards Report faulty equipment, poor lighting, broken furniture, or infection risks to your supervisor.

Standard 5 – Clinical Care

I understand the clinical needs of the person I’m caring for.

Monitor and report changes in health Observe residents for changes such as pain, confusion, mobility issues, or skin integrity and report promptly.

Follow safe care practices Support safe medication processes (without administering unless authorised), pressure injury prevention, and mobility support.

Provide care within your role and training Only perform tasks you are trained and authorised to do and seek guidance when unsure.

Standard 6 – Food and Nutrition

I make sure residents enjoy appetising and nutritious food every day.

Support individual dietary needs and preferences Follow dietary requirements such as allergies, texture‑modified diets, cultural preferences, and special nutrition needs.

Assist respectfully with eating and drinking Encourage independence, allow enough time for meals, and provide assistance calmly and respectfully when needed.

Report concerns about nutrition or hydration Report poor appetite, weight loss, swallowing difficulties, or dehydration to the appropriate staff member.

Standard 7 – The Residential Community

We work together to build a connected residential community.

Encourage social participation Support residents to join activities, outings, or social interactions based on their interests and abilities.

Support smooth transitions Provide reassurance and information when residents move rooms, return from hospital, or experience changes in care.

Promote respectful relationships Treat residents, families, and colleagues with respect and support positive communication and inclusion.

12. Distinguishing between care and support

Concepts of care: (LG p15) Connect

Care carries the concept of doing things for someone that they cannot do themselves to make them comfortable.

Support is about empowering a person to be as independent as they can be.

23. Restrictive practice

23. Restrictive practices involve restricting the freedom of movement that a person has, and there are strict requirements governing the use of restrictive practices. (LG p40) Connect CHCAGE013 And ConnectCHCDIS020 *CHCDIS020*

25. Types of restrictive practices

Connect

25. 5 Types of restrictive practices (LG p40)

  • Chemical restraint - This involves the use of a medication with the purpose of influencing a person's behaviour. (identified under NDIS and QLD legislation)
  • Environmental restraint - involves restricting free access to the person's available environment with the purpose of influencing behaviour.-(identified under NDIS)
  • Mechanical restraint - use of a device to restrict or prevent movement to influence a client's behaviour (identified under NDIS and QLD legislation)
  • Physical restraint -using physical force to restrict or prevent the movement of all or part of a client's body to influence client behaviour. (identified under NDIS and QLD legislation)
  • Seclusion - involves confining a client within a space or room where they are unable to exit voluntarily at any time with the purpose of influencing their behaviour. (identified under NDIS and QLD legislation)
  • Containment (identified under QLD legislation)
  • Restricting access (identified under QLD legislation)

*CHCAGE013* / *CHCDIS020*

26. Parameters for the use of restrictive practices

26. Parameters for the use of restrictive practices. (LG p41 ) Connect

  1. Only use restrictive practices as a last option, after trying other behavior strategies and recording their impact.
  2. If we're thinking about using restrictive practices, there must be a behaviour support plan (PSB)
  3. We need permission from the person or their decision maker to use restrictive practices.
  4. A healthcare professional who is approved must know the person well and have assessed them as a risk to themselves or others. We must write all of this down.
  5. If we use a restraint, we have to watch the person for any bad effects and make sure they're doing okay.
  6. We need to keep an eye on how well the restrictive practice is working.
  7. If we have to use a restrictive practice, it should be the one that limits the person the least, and we should only use it for the shortest time needed.
  8. If we're using chemical restraint , it must be done by a doctor or nurse who can prescribe medicine after a assessment. This must be written in the person's care plan.

*CHCAGE013*

29. New/contemporary view of living arrangements for those receiving Aged Care support

The traditional view of aged care has mainly focused on placing elderly people within an institutional setting. Aged people have been segregated from the rest of society and grouped into these settings, with little exposure to the other generations

30. Contemporary approaches to aged care - Some innovative concepts

30. Contemporary approaches to aged care - Some innovative concepts

  • (Small-scale Domestic Living: Creates a home-like atmosphere for residents to do things as they would in their own homes.
  • Dementia Villages: Involves houses in a village setting with retail stores, offering a familiar environment for those with dementia.
  • Bidyadanga Dementia Pilot Program: Supports Indigenous peoples to live in their community, strengthening local health workforce through education and empowerment.
  • Shared Housing Arrangements: 6-10 people share a home with a communal kitchen, living room, and support from community care services.
  • Teaching and Research Aged Care Service: Combines aged care services with teaching in a single environment.
  • Social and Care Farming: Involves normal farming activities to promote positive mental and physical health.
  • Cottage and Home-like Respite: Provides respite care in purpose-built cottage homes.
  • Intergenerational Models: Encourages elderly individuals to live near the general public, fostering interactions across age ranges. For instance, locating aged care next to a school promotes joint activities like art, music, and cooking classes.

*CHCAGE013* Connect

Contemporary view on disability support, including the identity model

A modern approach to disability support, including the identity model, means providing personalized assistance in places chosen by the person. It focuses on inclusion, accessibility, and empowering individuals with disabilities. The identity model seeks to define disability in a positive way based on the real experiences of people with disabilities. *CHCDIS020*

31. Separating the elderly from the mainstream of society and grouping them together

31. Separating the elderly from the mainstream of society and grouping them together (LG p17)

  • Keeping elderly people separate from the rest of society can lead to age discrimination, ageism and stereotyping and unfair judgments.
  • It can create a gap between generations, with young people missing out on the wisdom and care of older folks, and older people feeling lonely without the energy of the young.
  • We might lose chances for people to help and comfort each other.
  • Older folks might feel like their lives don't have a purpose and are empty.
  • It can cause divisions and disconnections based on age.

*CHCAGE013*

32. Negative attitudes and stereotypes (LG p90

Video: Hidden Attitudes on Ageing
The video file still needs to be added here.

32. Connect

  • Ageism - Being stereotyped and not treated well based on negative beliefs about what it means to be older, which limits choice and undermines self-esteem. Example - when someone thinks that older people can't learn new things, and as a result, they aren't allowed to do certain jobs.
  • Paternalism - Where those in authority restrict the freedoms of people who are dependent on them, supposedly in that person’s interest. Example - when we stop an older person from doing something they want to do because we're worried it might hurt them.
  • Stigma - When someone is seen in a negative way because of a certain attribute i.e. age. Being defined by a characteristic rather than being seen as a unique individual. - Example - when people treat you with disrespect because you're getting older and they believe you're becoming a burden to society.

Misconceptions - There are a lot of misunderstandings about ageing that lead to unfair treatment of older people. Two common myths are:

“Older people are a burden on society.”This isn’t true. Older people give a lot back to the community. They donate money, volunteer their time, and share valuable life experience (Queensland Government, 2016).

“All older people will get dementia.”While some older adults do develop dementia, most older Australians stay mentally sharp and have normal cognitive function (Roger, 2021).

*CHCAGE013*

37. FUNDING (LG p50)

Connect - Funding

CHCAGE013 Connect

Australian Government provides funding for aged care through grants, subsidies, and program funding. Aged individuals may contribute financially if able. A new funding model, AN-ACC, was introduced on October 1, 2022, impacting provider funding to better cover care costs.

AN-ACC class, determined by an assessment tool, guides funding for residential aged care. For home care, funding through CHSP or HCP is determined by assessment from Aged Care Assessment Teams (ACAT). Different care levels receive varying amounts, e.g., Level 1 is $9,179.75 per year. Clients work with chosen providers to decide fund allocation, and they may contribute if financially able.

38. Issues concerning Aged Care and Community support

Connect

Connect

  • Changing Demographics: There are more elderly people, and what they want from Aged Care is changing too.
  • Workforce Challenges: With more elderly people needing help, the staff have a heavier workload.
  • Aging Workforce: Many workers in this field are getting older, and we need to attract younger people to join.
  • Adequate Funding: We need enough money to hire staff who can meet everyone's needs.
  • Technology Advancements: Using technology, like devices that help clients be more independent, can improve the industry.
  • Access Difficulties: Some older folks struggle to get the help they need from the Aged Care system.
  • Low-Quality Care and Mistreatment: Some people receive care that isn't good enough, and there are cases of abuse.
